findings.title: Multiple crypto providers are now silently tolerated, with non-deterministic tie-breaking
findings.body: detectProvider() no longer throws when more than one CryptoProvider is found on the classpath; it just sorts by order() and picks the first. All three in-tree providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider) return order() == 200, and Stream.sorted() is stable, so when two of them are on the classpath the selected provider is decided purely by ServiceLoader/classpath discovery order. The removed IllegalStateException was the guard that caught exactly this misconfiguration; now a deployment that accidentally has both the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider and the FIPS provider on the classpath can silently run non-FIPS crypto (or vice versa) with no error, and the behaviour can change between environments or build layouts. Either keep failing when two providers share the same order, or give the real providers distinct orders and log at WARN/ERROR when more than one is present.

findings.title: order() added as a non-default interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI in keycloak-common. Adding the abstract method `int order();` is a source- and binary-incompatible change: any out-of-tree implementation (and, per the PR description, the authz-client copy maintained in the keycloak-client repository which compiles against a released keycloak-common) will no longer compile, and pre-compiled implementations will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts the providers. Declaring it as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or some neutral baseline) keeps compatibility while still allowing the new provider to lower/raise its precedence.

findings.title: logger.debugf() called with a dynamically built string as the format
findings.body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes runtime-constructed text as the format string. If any ignored provider class name ever contains a '%' the formatter will throw or produce garbage, and static analysis/IDE format checks cannot validate it. Use `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` (or logger.debug(Object)). The message should also be built lazily (guarded by isDebugEnabled) and, given that silently ignoring a crypto provider used to be a fatal error, logged at WARN rather than DEBUG so misconfigured classpaths are visible. The message also ends with a dangling ", ".

findings.title: Dead code: two ASN1Encoder instances created and discarded in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) build encoders whose results are thrown away; the actual DER sequence is produced from freshly created encoders on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect and only confuse readers (they look like they are part of the encoding). They should be removed.

findings.title: integerToBytes silently truncates integers larger than the expected signature half-length
findings.body: When `qLength < bytes.length` the method keeps only the low-order qLength bytes of the BigInteger, silently discarding high-order bytes. The BouncyCastle-based implementation this replaces uses BigIntegers.asUnsignedByteArray(len, value), which raises an error when the value does not fit. With this implementation a DER signature containing an r/s value wider than the algorithm's half-length (corrupt input, or a mismatch between the key curve and the declared ES* algorithm) is converted to a wrong concatenated R||S value instead of failing, which turns a detectable error into a silently invalid signature. It should throw IOException when the value does not fit in qLength bytes.

findings.title: Indefinite-length encoding (-1 from readLength) is not handled by readInteger/readSequence
findings.body: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80). readInteger() passes that value straight to read(length), which executes `new byte[-1]` and throws NegativeArraySizeException - an unchecked exception escaping a method that declares IOException, so callers that catch IOException will not handle it. readSequence() with a -1 length simply skips the while loop and returns an empty list, hiding the malformed input. Malformed or BER-encoded input (asn1derToConcatenatedRS is called with externally supplied bytes) should be rejected with a clear IOException instead.

findings.title: Test uses the default EC curve for ES384/ES512 and never validates the produced DER with a verifier
findings.body: The key pair is generated once with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` using the JDK default curve (P-256 on current JDKs), so testES384/testES512 sign with a P-256 key while asserting against signature lengths 96/132. The round-trip assertion still passes because r/s are simply zero-padded, so the real P-384/P-521 r/s widths produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER are never exercised. Additionally the test only asserts rsConcat == rsConcat2; it never feeds the DER output of concatenatedRSToASN1DER into Signature.verify(), which is the actual production use of that method (JWS signature verification), so an encoder that produces structurally parseable but non-DER output would not be caught. Generate keys with the curve matching each algorithm (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded DER with a JCA Signature.
